`precision: 40` in the front matter applies to every cell on this page, so
everything below is computed to 40 decimal digits.

## Special values

```{gp}
zeta(2)
```

```{gp}
Pi^2/6
```

Euler's evaluation, to the last digit. At odd arguments there is no such
closed form, and $\zeta(3)$ is simply a number:

```{gp}
zeta(3)
```

At negative integers the values are rational, and they are Bernoulli numbers
in disguise: $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n+1}/(n+1)$.

```{gp}
[zeta(-1), -bernfrac(2)/2 * 1.]
```

```{gp}
[zeta(-3), -bernfrac(4)/4 * 1.]
```

## On the critical line

$\zeta(1/2 + it)$ is complex, and its size is what the Riemann hypothesis is
about:

```{gp}
zeta(1/2 + 14*I)
```

Small, but not zero — the first zero sits just above $t = 14$:

```{gp}
lfunzeros(1, [0, 40])
```

`{gp} #lfunzeros(1, [0, 40])` zeros below height 40. Feeding one back in
gives zero to working precision:

```{gp}
abs(zeta(1/2 + I * lfunzeros(1, [0, 20])[1])) < 1e-30
```

## The L-function machinery

`lfun` treats $\zeta$ as one $L$-function among many — `1` is the Riemann
zeta function, and a Dirichlet character or an elliptic curve goes in the
same slot:

```{gp}
[lfun(1, 2), zeta(2)]
```

The $L$-function of $X_0(11)$ at the centre of its critical strip, which
vanishes to order zero because the curve has rank zero:

```{gp}
E = ellinit([0, -1, 1, -10, -20]);
lfun(E, 1)
```

## The Euler product

Truncated over the primes below $10^5$, it approaches $\zeta(2)$ from below:

```{gp}
prodeuler(p = 2, 10^5, 1/(1 - p^-2))
```

```{gp}
zeta(2) - prodeuler(p = 2, 10^5, 1/(1 - p^-2))
```
